question: A 5-year-old unvaccinated boy arrives in the emergency department with high fever, drooling, inspiratory stridor, and sitting rigidly upright with his neck extended. He appears toxic and frightened. His oxygen saturation is 94% on air. What is the single most important IMMEDIATE action?

answers.text: Perform direct throat examination with a tongue depressor to confirm the diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is absolutely contraindicated. Direct throat examination in suspected epiglottitis — even with a tongue depressor — can precipitate complete airway obstruction through laryngospasm and reflex vagal stimulation. The child must NEVER be asked to open the mouth or have anything inserted orally before the airway is secured in a controlled environment.

answers.text: Obtain a lateral neck X-ray immediately to confirm the thumbprint sign before treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: When clinical epiglottitis is suspected, investigations — including X-ray — must NOT be performed before the airway is secured. Moving the child, placing him supine for X-ray, or any agitation can trigger complete obstruction. The lateral neck X-ray (thumbprint sign) is confirmatory but NEVER takes priority over airway security.

answers.text: Keep the child calm and upright, call for senior anaesthetist and ENT surgeon, and arrange controlled intubation in the operating theatre

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The priority is to avoid any action that agitates the child (which worsens airway obstruction) while urgently summoning the team needed to secure the airway. Controlled orotracheal intubation under inhalational anaesthesia in theatre, with ENT and a surgeon ready to perform emergency tracheostomy, is the gold standard. Do not attempt IV cannulation, examination, or investigations until the airway is secure.

answers.text: Start nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone immediately as for croup

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone are treatments for croup (viral laryngotracheobronchitis), not epiglottitis. Epiglottitis is a bacterial supraglottic infection (Haemophilus influenzae type b) requiring airway security and intravenous antibiotics (ceftriaxone). Croup treatments will not address the bacterial cellulitis of the epiglottis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The golden rule in epiglottitis: DO NOT examine the throat, DO NOT lay the child down, DO NOT attempt IV access or X-rays before the airway is secured. Summon the team and secure the airway in a controlled setting.

Excellent. In epiglottitis, the primary imperative is to keep the child calm and upright while urgently preparing for controlled airway securing. Every invasive or agitating action risks precipitating fatal complete obstruction.
